AKM Nazrul Islam Rokonuddin Mahmood. Abdur Razzaque Senior Advocates with Ehsan A. Siddiq, SA Nabi and Mir Ahmed Bin Quasem, Advocates ------ For the Respondents.
parties:
Social Islamic Bank Limited and others ------ Defendant-Appellant
Vs.
Major (Retd) Dr. Md. Rezaul Haque  ------ Plaintiff-Respondents
full_judgment:
Md. Rezaul Hasan J: This Appeal under Order XLIII Rule 1(r) of the Code of Civil Procedure (CPC). has been preferred by the Social Islamic Bank Ltd. (SIBL) and five others being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the impugned Order No. 08 dated 26-10-2011 passed by the 5th Court of Joint District Judge, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 422 of 2011 allowing the application filed by the plaintiff- respondent under Order XXXIX, Rule 1 & 2 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure (CPC) and section 55 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877 and passing a temporary order of injunction in mandatory form directing the defendant Nos. 1-6 to serve the notice of the Board Meeting upon the plaintiff and to allow the plaintiff to act as a Director of the defendant No.1 Bank. 

 3. Facts leading to file this appeal, in brief, are that on 05-10-2011 the Plaintiff-Respondent has filed, on 15-07-1995, a Title Suit No. 422 of 2011 against the appellants stating,' inter alia, that the Social Islamic Bank Ltd. (SIBL), which is defendant No.1, has been registered as a public company limited by shares as per provisions of the Companies Act, 1994 and that the plaintiff is a sponsor director of the SIBL, holding 55,83,766 shares. The defendant No.1 (SIBL)is a banking company, defendant No.2 is the Chairman of the said Bank and the defendants No.2-6 are directors of the Bank. The defendant No.7-9, namely the Governor of Bangladesh Bank, the General Manager (BRPD). Bangladesh Bank and the Register, Joint Stock Companies and Firms are the pro-forma defendants. Plaintiff's further case is that since registration of the Bank he has been regularly attending the board meetings of the Bank and has been performing functions as member of different sub-committees and was the chairman of the audit committee in 2009- 2010; that by a notice dated 26-09-2011 an emergency meeting of the board of directors of SIBL was called on 28-09-2011; that there was no agenda in the said meeting to remove the plaintiff from the board of directors of SIBL, rather agenda NoA2 of the meeting was regarding discussion of the legal opinion of Barrister Mr. Rafiqul Haque and to take corrective measures for protecting interest of the Bank and of the shareholders; that at the time of discussion on agenda No. 42 defendant No.2, all on a sudden, made a comment that in the matter of renunciation of right shares in favour of IFIL (Islamic Finance and Investment Limited) the plaintiff might have some interest and he had invited opinion of director Sultan Mahmud Chowdhury, who has opined that the plaintiff had connivance in the matter of renunciation of shares in favour of IFIL and Mr. Sultan Mahmood Chowdhury had proposed to remove the plaintiff from the board of directors. Accordingly, the defendants Nos.2-6, pursuant to a pre-plan, had removed the plaintiff from the board of directors of Social Islamic Bank Ltd. (SIBL) in the 258th meeting of the board of directors, which is totally illegal. The plaintiff further states that, as per provisions of section 106 of the Companies Act, 1994, in order to remove a director from his office an extra ordinary resolution will have to be adopted and that the board of directors has no power or authority to remove another director and that all these acts and deeds were done at the behest of defendant No.2 to take entire control of the SIBL in the hands of defendant Nos.2-6. He also states that the board had no power even to remove him with reference to section 108(2) of the Companies Act read with article 65.3 (Clause 1C of the undertaking) or Article 82.9 of the Articles of Association (AoA) of the Bank. He then states that the plaintiff had never interfered in the administration or management of the business of banking, nor he had taken any loan from the Bank, nor did any act contrary to sariah and, as such, there was no scope to declare that his office has fallen vacant. But the plaintiff has been removed from the board of directors of SIBL. His further case is that, after his removal from the board of SIBL the board has issued a notice dated 28-9-2011 convening its 259th meeting on the following day, that is on 29-9-2011, but no notice of the 259th board meeting was served upon the plaintiff. Hence, he asserts, that the said notice dated 28-9-2011 convening 259th board meeting is absolutely illegal, irregular, unlawful and ineffective. Accordingly, he has prayed for declaring that his removal in the 258th board meeting dated 28-9-2011 was done in violation of section 106 of the Companies Act, 1994 and that the decision of his removal from the office of director was illegal, ultravires and not binding on him and to declare further that he is still continuing as a lawful director of the SIBL. He has also asked for further declaration to the effect that the notice dated 28-9-2011 for co-option of a new director in the board meeting dated 29-9-2011 is illegal and ultravires. 

 4. In the pending suit, the plaintiff has also filed an application, on 17-10-2011, under Order XXXIX Rule 1 and 2 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure (CPC), stating almost similar facts and praying for a mandatory injunction to the effect that- 

 6. After hearing both the parties the Joint District Judge, 5th Court, Dhaka, by order dated 26-10-2011, has allowed petition for injunction in mandatory form holding that the plaintiff shall have right to attend all the meetings and the defendants should issue all notices on him as usually treating him as a director of the Bank. Being aggrieved by this order dated 26-10-2011 the appellants has preferred the instant appeal before this court. 

 7. The learned Senior Advocate Mr. Rafique-ul-Haq alongwith Mr. Aminul Hoque and Ms. Dilara Khandaker, Advocates appearing for the appellants, having placed the memorandum of appeal and other documents on record before us, has taken us through the case and submits that there are consistent decisions of almost all the jurisdictions that the Court should not interfere with the internal management of a company by issuing an order of injunction. He also strenuously argued that, in passing the impugned order, the trial Court has restored directorship to the plaintiff that has ceased at least one month before the date of passing the impugned order and this order of the trial Court restoring status-quo anti is absolutely illegal. In support of his contention the learned Advocate has referred to the cases of Nurul Islam vs Khatibuddin Ahmed: 56 DLR 545; Abul Hayat Sunu vs M A Reja: 47 DLR 170; Abdul Jalil vs Abu Bakr Siddique: 35 DLR (AD) 43 and Mr. Mainul Hosein vs Mr. Anwar Hossain: 4 BLT (AD) 76. He next submits that, although in the resolution adopted in the 258th board meeting, dated 28-9-2011, the word removal has been used it was indeed an act of recording 'vacation of office' of the plaintiff as would be apparent from the fact of referring to section 108 of sub-section (2) of the Companies Act, 1994 and article 65.3 paragraph 1 (c) of the undertaking and Article 82.09 of the Articles of Association (AoA) in the said resolution. He also submits that, as the board of directors has power to record vacation of office as per Article 65.3 (paragraph 1(C) of the undertaking) and 82.09, so mere error in using the proper term would not pollute the Board's power to record a decision regarding the vacation of office. In support of his contention the learned advocate has referred to a decision reported in 47 DLR (AD) 1: Col. Md. Hashmat Ali (Retd.) vs Government of Bangladesh. The learned advocate, then drawing our attention to paragraph 1 (c) of the undertaking forming part of Article 65.3 of the AoA, submits that the Board, which is better posted with the relevant facts, is the sole authority to decide as to whether a director has acted in breach of the undertaking and that the power exercised by the board, apparently to record the vacation of office, is quite within the ambit of the board's power conferred on it by the AoA of the SIBL. He continues maintaining that, as recorded in the concerned minutes of agenda No. 42 of the 258thboard meeting, apparently the board has taken a decision for violation of the undertaking and simply recorded the vacation of his office as per provisions of article 82.09 of the AoA of the SIBL. As such, it is a clear case of vacation of office recorded in the said resolution and since there is source of power vested in the directors, so mere mentioning of the word 'removal' could not make the resolution illegal, he asserts. He also submits, referring to the renunciation form, that the form of renunciation contains a date being 6-5-2011 at the top right hand comer and shows that the signature of the renouncee was verified on 4-5-2011 and that the price of the right shares (at face value) was deposited in the Bank on 5-5-2011, as such, on the face of these documents a case of anti-dated fraudulent transaction, at the behest of the plaintiff, has been revealed and that justifies the action taken. He finally submits that, in passing the impugned order the trial Court has given the full relief pending disposal of the suit and this is contrary to the law declared in the case of Government vs Md. Matiur Rahman: 3 LG (AD) (2006) 25. Accordingly, the learned advocate concludes that, the impugned order has been passed without appreciating the facts and law involved in this case and in violation of the principles guiding discretion in the matter of granting temporary injunction. Hence, the impugned order is liable to be set-aside and the appeal be allowed. 

 8. Mr. AKM Nazrul Islam, Mr. Rokonuddin Mahmood and Mr. Abdur Razzaqu, Senior Advocates along with Mr. Ehsan A Siddiq, SA Nabi and Mr. Mir Ahmed Bin Quasem, advocates appeared for the plaintiff-respondent. They have referred to the documents annexed to the petition for injunction filed by the respondent, the petition for vacating the stay, the additional paper book filed by the respondent and to other documents and materials on record. 

 10. The learned senior advocate Mr. AKM Nazrul Islam mainly submits that the act of renunciation is absolutely legal and according to the Securities & Exchange Commission (Rights Issue) Rules, 2006 and that the board cannot exercise its power arbitrarily without affording the plaintiff- director an opportunity to explain his position. He further submits that when there is a wrong there must be some remedy and the trial Court has simply remidied the wrong done to plaintiff, therefore, it has committed no illegality in passing the impugned order. The learned advocate has also referred to a decision reported in 31 DLR (1995) 5: Shamsul Huda vs Jalaluddin Ahmed wherein a' Bench of this Division has held, to record an execption to the law laid down in Foss vs Harbottle, that "for the protection of right of individual members of a company can sue. The Court below wrongly decided that the plaintiff has no cause of action, just because he was not suing in the name of the company in accordance with the law laid down in Foss vs Harbottle". We shall advert to this decision at the appropriate place. 

 11. The learned Senior Advocate Mr. Rokonuddin Mahmood, drawing our attention to the resolution and the notice of the 258th Board meeting, mainly submits that there was no agenda in the notice to remove the plaintiff from the board of directors. He then submits that, it was a proposal for removal of the plaintiff from the board of directors and this is clearly evident from the minutes itself and it has been recorded in the minutes that some directors have taken decision to remove the plaintiff. So this is a clear case of 'removal' of the plaintiff on the proposal and decision of the members of the SIBL board of directors and the verbal submission of the learned advocate for the appellant that it was a case of using wrong term cannot be accepted in the absence of any materials on record to substantiate such verbal submission. Rather, apparently, this decision of removal from the board, taken in the 258th (emergency) meeting of the board, held on 28-9-2011, has been taken in clear violation of section 106 of the of the Companies Act, 1994 that lays down a special procedure for removal of a director requiring an extraordinary resolution to be adopted, by two-third majority of the members present, in a general meeting summoned for that purpose. Board of directors has no power to remove the plaintiff director, more so without any agenda or any notice expressing any intention to adopt such a resolution. As such, he submits, that the impugned resolution removing the plaintiff is prima facie ultravires, a nullity and void as initio. Hence the trial Court has committed no illegality in passing the impugned order. He then submits that, by a letter dated 03-10-2011 issued by the General Manager BRPD of Bangladesh Bank the appellants were asked to show cause, within five days, under what authority they had removed the plaintiff from the office of the director. He finally submits that, it was the exclusive authority of Bangladesh Bank to remove a director, as authorised by section 46 of the Bank Companies Act, 1991. Next, drawing our attention to section 2 of the Bank Companies Act, 1991 (BCA) the learned Advocate further submits that, the BCA being a special law it will prevail over the provisions of the Companies Act, 1994, and that, specific provisions having been made in the BCA for removal of a Bank director by Bangladesh Bank and Bangladesh Bank having not taken any step against the plaintiff-respondent, the appellants had no authority to take any decision to remove the plaintiff-respondent. On all these grounds, he concludes, the impugned order was quite proper, hence the same do not warrant any interference by this Court and the stay granted by this Court is liable to be vacated along with appropriate direction to restore the status-quo that was prevailing on the date of passing of the order impugned in this appeal. 

 14. Now looking at the minutes of the 258th emergency board meeting, held on 28-9-2011, as pointed out by the senior counsel Mr. Mahmood, we find that the plaintiff-respondent was removed on the basis of a proposal of the director Mr. Alhaj Sultan Mahmood Chowdhury to remove the plaintiff-respondent from the board of directors, recording some allegations against the plaintiff, and all other directors accepted the proposal for removal. The relevant motion, as recorded in the minutes reads as follows: "Alhaj Sultan Mahmood Chowdhury, honourable Director proposed 12 remove Major (Retd.) Dr. Md. Rezaul Haque, honourable Director from the Board of Directors and Alhaj Nasiruddin, honourable Director and Mr. Md. Shah Alam, honourable Director seconded the proposal, removal decision may be taken as empowered in pursuance to Companies Act, 1994, Section # 108(2) read with Article No.# 65(3)-1C and Article No. # 82.9 of Articles of Association of the Bank. All other directors accepted the proposal for removal." Accordingly, the following resolution was adopted in that meeting, namely- "(a) Major (Retd.) Dr. Md. Rezaul Haque, honourable Director is hereby removed in pursuance to Companies Act, 1994, section # 108(2) read with Articles No. # 65(3)-1C and Article No. # 82.9 of Articles of Association of the Bank with immediate effect from the position of Director of Social Islami Bank Limited for his unethical and oath-violating activities by renunciation and sale of Foreigner's Shares in collaboration with the Islamic Finance and Investment Limited (IFIL) which is contrary/derogatory to the objectives or interest of the Bank and Shariah". 

 15. Prima facie, the concerned minutes shows that a motion was moved by a director to remove the plaintiff from the office of director, which was accepted as such by all the directors and plaintiff was removed from his office with immediate effect, vide the resolution quoted above, although the defendant-appellants can adduce evidence, at the time of trial, to prove that in substance the decision taken was one for recording vacation of office as per section 108(2) read with the Artices 65(3) and 82.9 of the AoA of the SIBL, as recorded in the concerned resolution. However, at this stage this Court will simply consider as to whether the plaintiff- respondent has been able to make out an arguable case. 

 16. Since, prima facie this appears to be a case of removal of a director, so the board of directors, in order to implement its decision to remove the plaintiff-respondent, could have further resolved to convene a general or extraordinary general meeting to consider and adopt an extraordinary resolution for removal of the plaintiff as per provision of section 106 of the Companies Act, 1994. Similar provision for removal of a director has also been made in Article 92 of the Articles of Association (AoA) of the SIBL that provides that, the company may, by an extra ordinary resolution, remove any director before the expiration of his period of office. This article has been incorporated in terms of the provisions of section 106 of the Companies Act, 1994. But in this particular case apparently the respondents did not follow the procedure laid down in article 92 of the AoA of the SIBL or in section 106 of the Companies Act, 1994. However, whether this is a mere case of using wrong terminology, as was argued by the learned senior advocate appearing for the appellant, has to be proved by the defendant- appellant at the time of trial. 

 17. Besides, the office of a director of the SIBL is subject to retirement by rotation. This being the fact we are also of the view that, in this case, the balance of convenience and inconvenience is in favour of granting injunction and that the plaintiff would suffer irreparable loss in the absence of an appropriate order of injunction. We also consider the decision reported in AIR 1995 (Guj) 93: Jivanbhai vs Bhavanjee is of immense persuasive value and has declared the correct position of law. It has been held in that case that "it is true that when there is contest or controversy between the parties about the status, the Court normally refrains from granting the final relief at an interlocutory stage, but Court is certainly entitled to scan the so-called defence about the denial of status of tenancy raised by the other side. Otherwise, Court would be encouraging the dishonest defence and allowing the party to live at the mercy of the opponent till his rights are finalized. It is very easy for the opponent in any case to deny the status of one party who goes to Court after doing illegal acts and then to contend that no final relief be granted at an interlocutory stage. The Court in such situation cannot sit and watch the proceedings as a silent spectator and show its helplessness". We respectfully endorse this view. Simultaneously, we have also considered the decision reported in 3 LG (2006) AD 25: Government vs Md. Matiur Rahman, wherein the apex court: in a writ matter, has held that, "ad-interim order amounting to full relief should not be granted." The law thus declared by the apex Court is, indeed, a settled position of law guiding the practice and procedure in writ matters. But, the case before us is a civil matter and the question of granting or refusing petition for injunction is guided by different considerations, namely- (I) whether the petitioner has been able to make out a prima facie case, (II) in which side the balance of convenience and inconvenience is titled and (III) whether the petitioner would suffer irreparable loss in the case of not granting an order of injunction. There are other principles that has shaped the practice and procedure in this respect, but obviously it would amount to asking us a wrong question, in a civil matter, as to whether the Court below has given full relief by the impugned order passed under Order XXXIX, rule 1 & 2 read with section 151 of the CPE. Hence, we find that the decision reported in 3 LG (2006) (AD) 25 is liable to be distinguished and is not applicable to this case. 

 18. Thereafter, adverting to the contentions that the plaintiff-respondent has committed some illegalities or resorted to some fraudulent practices, as has been recorded in the minutes of the 258th (emergency) Board meeting pirating to agenda No. 42 and as regards the form of renunciation, we consider this as a. matter concerning the merit of the case to be decided by the trial Court upon considering the evidence that may be adduced by the contending parties. Similarly, the correspondence by and between SIBL and Bangladesh Bank are also to be looked, if the pleadings permits, at the time of trial. 

 19. It is also advisable, as has been held in the case reported in 4 BLT (AD) 76: Mr. Moinul Hossein vs Mr. Anwar Hossain, that the Court should not interfere by granting injunction where the internal management and functioning of the company may be affected: This decision of the apex Court has not only laid down the consistent views expressed by the courts under various jurisdiction, more so this decision is binding on this Division as per Article III of the Constitution. Learned senior advocate Mr. Huq has relied on this decision when he was very impressively assailing the legality and propriety of the impugned decision. But, the facts of this case [4 BLT (AD) 76] is liable to be distinguished from the facts of the case before us, while we find nothing apparent from the record before us as to how the impugned decision would affect the internal management or functioning of the SIBL, and this again remains to be the onus of the defendant-appellant to prove their case at the time of trial. Besides, we have looked into the statement of the company secretary recorded in Board Memo No. 514 of 2010, dated 9-8-2011, quoted herein before, only to decide about the prima-facie case. We shall, however, make it clear that this statement is indeed a report made by the company secretary for appraisal of the Board. We have not treated this as admission made by the company (SIBL) or by the defendants-appellants, who are always entitled to ascertain the correctness of such a report. Nor we have regarded this report to operate as an estoppel against the defendant-appellants.in stating their case. 

 20. We have rather considered the views expressed in the cases, cited by the learned counsel for the respondent Mr. Abdur Razzaque, as more relevant to the situation of the case before us. We, therefore respectfully endorse the view that, "the rule against interference by Court with internal management of the companies is not applicable to cases of infringement of individual membership rights as distinguished from corporate membership right" as has been held in the case of Avant he Explosives P. Ltd., reported in (1987) 69 Company Cases 301. Accordingly, we are of the view that the suit brought by the plaintiff to have it declared that his removal from the office of the director of SIBL is illegal, ultravires, malafide and that the notice to co-opt another director in his place is one pertaining to the individual right of the plaintiff-director and this has no nexus with the internal management or functioning of the company. Here, we also accept the ratio of the case reported in AIR (38) 1951 Madras 542, cited on behalf of the respondent. Besides, the principle laid down in the case reported in 31 DLR 5 (paragraph. 11) also lends support to our this view. 

 24. Before parting of, we must record that the plaintiff-respondent has filed one injunction petition and another petition for vacating stay and submitted that, taking advantage of the stay order passed by this court, the Bank was proceeding with undue haste to curtail valuable rights of the plaintiff respondent while the appeal was pending. We have kept these two petitions with the record for consideration at the time of hearing of the appeal and the learned lawyers of both sides have agreed that this Court can pass consequential order in accordance with the fate of the appeal.
